Beau's Homepage

Featured Research

  • The pupil response to perceptual switches: What happens when you ignore them Featured Research

    The pupil has been found to dilate after switches in bistable perception, prompting the suggestion that norepinephrine-based neuromodulation plays a causal role in those switches. However, the pupil dilates in response to task-relevant events in general, and, in existing work, perceptual switches were typically task-relevant (e.g., they had to be reported). As such, observed switch-related dilations may have reflected nonspecific task relevance rather than switch-specific processes. Here, we measured pupil responses to perceptual switches that were task-irrelevant.

  • Widespread lack of article accessibility policies among ecology and evolution journals Featured Research

    Recent work has illuminated huge inequities in academic publishing based on author demographics such as assumed gender, geography, language and prestige. Yet, little attention has been paid to the inequities that scientists with disabilities face. We reviewed the websites of 541 ecology and evolution journals to examine the extent to which they prompt authors to prepare accessible manuscripts. Here we show that nearly three-quarters of journals do not encourage authors to consider accessibility when preparing manuscripts. Existing guidelines focus primarily on colour-blind-friendly figures, which were mentioned almost twice as often as any other recommendation.

Projects

  • Displacement-based OKN analysis

    Displacement-based gaze processing for optokinetic nystagmus during perceptual bistability focusing on using horizontal displacement relative to vertical displacement as a proxy for perceived direction

  • Small Business Resilience in Colorado

    An attempt to create a composite resilience scores for small businesses in Colorado, including components such as cultural well-being, technological adoption, individual resilience, human capital, and financial and physical health

  • Velocity-based OKN analysis

    Velocity-based gaze processing for optokinetic nystagmus during perceptual bistability using velocity permutations and per-observer velocity threshold to identify perceptual switches

  • Mechanistic isolation of switch-related pupil response Dissertation!

    Introducing disparity-simulated perceptual switches to investigate the mechanisms underlying pupil responses accompanying spontaneous perceptual switches

Publications

  • Binocularly-Driven Neural Responses to Chromatic Interocular-Switch Rivalry

    Competing rivalrous neural representations can be resolved at several levels of the visual system. Sustained percepts during interocular-switch rivalry (ISR), in which rivalrous left- and right-eye stimuli swap between eyes several times a second, often are attributed to competing binocularly driven neural representations of each rivalrous stimulus. Here, a range of experimental conditions was tested that would change the colors seen if mediated by eye dominance but not if by competition between binocularly driven responses.

  • Effects of Knowledge on Bistable Perception of Structure-from-Motion

    We revisited a body of work that shows the occurrence of perceptual reversals to depend dramatically on the observer's knowledge that the input is, indeed, ambiguous: without such knowledge many observers in that work did not experience any reversals, in apparent conflict with the idea that reversals are inevitable. We used an ambiguous animation that allowed subjects to report perceptual reversals without realizing the ambiguity.

  • Fixational saccade inhibition and pupil dilation during self-paced limb movement preparation

    The researchers investigated how small involuntary eye movements change during preparation for self-initiated limb actions. They found that fixational saccade rates progressively decreased before hand and foot movements, then briefly increased afterward. Pupil dilation patterns showed similar timing. The study demonstrates that the magnitudes of fixational saccade rate modulation and of pupil size modulation are associated across motor actions, suggesting shared neural mechanisms controlling both responses during movement preparation independent of external stimuli.
